title: Woe to Those Who Seize Fields, and a Remnant Gathered
summary: Micah pronounces woe on powerful men who lie awake plotting how to seize their neighbors' fields and houses. God, in turn, plans a disaster against them from which they cannot escape, and they will lose their own land. The people tell Micah to stop preaching such things and would prefer a prophet who promises wine and strong drink. The chapter closes with God's promise to gather the remnant of Israel like a flock and lead them out, with their King going before them.
story: Chapter 1 described the disaster coming on Samaria and Judah; chapter 2 explains one of its main causes. Micah moves from idolatry to economics, from the high places to the fields. The land was God's gift to Israel's families, and Micah sees it being swallowed by the powerful. This chapter also introduces the conflict between Micah and the popular preachers of his day, which will return in chapter 3. At its end comes the first word of hope in the book, closing the first of Micah's three cycles of judgment and promise.
historical:
The eighth century BC was a time of economic change in both Israel and Judah. Wealth from trade and royal administration flowed to a class of officials and landowners, while small farmers, vulnerable to drought, taxation, and war, fell into debt. When debts could not be paid, fields and houses were seized, and families could lose their land for good. Isaiah, preaching in Jerusalem in the same years, pronounced woe on those who "add house to house and join field to field" in a similar spirit (Isaiah 5:8). Some archaeologists have pointed to changes in house sizes in Israelite towns during this period as evidence of growing inequality, though how to interpret such evidence is debated.

Micah, from a country town in the Shephelah, may have seen these seizures firsthand. The coming Assyrian invasion (culminating for Judah in Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC) would strip the land-grabbers of the very fields they had taken, as verses 3 to 5 warn.
cultural:
In Israel's law, land was not an ordinary commodity. Each tribe, clan, and family had received its portion by lot when Israel entered Canaan (Joshua 13-19), and the land ultimately belonged to God, who said, "it is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me" (Leviticus 25:23). A family's field was its inheritance, the basis of its livelihood and its place among God's people. The law provided for land to return to its original family in the Year of Jubilee (Leviticus 25), and it forbade moving a neighbor's boundary stone (Deuteronomy 19:14). The story of Naboth, who refused to sell his vineyard to King Ahab because it was his fathers' inheritance, shows how seriously this was taken (1 Kings 21).

Verse 5 threatens that the land-grabbers will have "no one in the assembly of the LORD to divide the land by lot". When God restores his people, they will have no share in the redistribution. The women and children driven from their homes (verse 9) were the most vulnerable, often widows and orphans whose protection the law specifically commanded (Exodus 22:22-24). Taking the cloak from passersby (verse 8) recalls the law that a poor man's cloak taken in pledge must be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26-27).
literary: The chapter opens with a woe oracle, a form used for funeral laments, and builds on a pattern of fitting punishment. The rich devise evil on their beds (verse 1); God devises disaster against them (verse 3), using the same verb. They seize fields; their own fields will be divided among traitors. Verses 6 to 11 are a dispute: the people's words are quoted ("Do not preach") and answered. The word for preach here literally means to drip, perhaps suggesting a prophet's words dripping like rain, or used mockingly for dribbling speech. It appears five times in these verses. The false preacher Micah imagines is a "man of wind", a play on the word ruach, which means wind and also spirit. The chapter ends abruptly with a promise of gathering (verses 12 and 13), shifting from judgment to hope without transition, a pattern that recurs in the book.

outline.t: Woe to those who plot to seize fields and houses
God's counter-plan: the land-grabbers lose their land
Do not preach: the people silence the prophet
The crimes of the powerful and the preacher they want
The remnant gathered, the breaker and the King go before them

doctrines.note: The laws about land, inheritance, and the cloak in pledge were meant to keep every family rooted and secure under God's ownership. Micah shows that breaking them is not a technicality but an attack on the people God gave the land to.
God's judgment fits the crime: those who plan evil on their beds face a disaster God has planned, and those who took fields lose their own. God is not indifferent to economic injustice.
The gathering of the remnant (verses 12 and 13) shows that judgment is not God's final purpose. He will gather his scattered people like a shepherd and go before them as King.

words.note: Chamad, to desire or covet. The verb of the tenth commandment: "You shall not covet your neighbor’s house" (Exodus 20:17). Micah shows where coveting leads when it has power behind it: they covet fields, then seize them. Desire becomes robbery.

Nachalah, inheritance. The family land received from God and passed down through generations. It was more than property; it was a family's share in God's promise. To take a man's nachalah was to cut him off from his place among God's people.

Nataph, to drip, and by extension to preach or prophesy. Used five times in verses 6 and 11. The popular preachers tell Micah to stop dripping words of doom, while they themselves would gladly drip words about wine and strong drink. The word may carry a note of contempt.

Parats, to break through. Used twice in verse 13 for the one who breaks open the way and the people breaking through the gate. The picture is of a leader who opens a way out of captivity, with the LORD himself going at the head.

christ: Micah 2:12-13 pictures God gathering his scattered people like a shepherd and a King who goes before them, breaking open the way. The New Testament presents Jesus as the good shepherd who gathers his flock, calls his sheep by name, and leads them out (John 10:3-4, 10:16). Some older interpreters, both Jewish and Christian, read "the one who breaks open the way" as a messianic figure; others see the breaker simply as the LORD himself, since the verse ends with the LORD as their leader. Either way the pattern fits Jesus, who went ahead of his people through death and opened the way to God (Hebrews 10:19-20). The chapter's concern for the poor stripped of their homes also anticipates Jesus' warnings against those who devour widows' houses (Mark 12:40).

hard.q: Were the land-grabbers breaking any law, or just taking advantage of a legal system?
hard.a: Micah's charge may cover both. Some seizures were probably outright fraud or violence, but many may have been technically legal, through foreclosure on debts or rigged courts (Micah 3:11 speaks of judges taking bribes). Micah's point is that legality is not the measure. God's law aimed at keeping every family on its inheritance, and the Jubilee and redemption laws were designed to prevent permanent dispossession. Using legal means to defeat the law's purpose is still injustice in God's eyes. Interpreters differ on how directly these laws should shape modern economics, but the principle that power must not be used to strip the vulnerable of their livelihood is clear.

questions: Micah condemns those who plot evil on their beds and carry it out because they have the power. Where do you have power that could be used to take advantage of others?
The people wanted a preacher who would promise wine and strong drink. What messages do you prefer to hear, and what might you be refusing to hear?
God promises to gather the scattered and go before them. Who are the scattered in your community, and how might you join God's work of gathering?
